amendments.rule: **Where a privative `מִן` + infinitive construct is recast as a negative result clause, the preposition takes the frame's function words and the infinitive takes its supplied subject.** The ASV writes *that it cannot save*, *so that he will not hear*, *that I should give*. The complementizer and the negation are what the `מִן` contributes and stay with it, including a *cannot* that fuses that negation with the modal and so cannot be divided; the supplied subject pronoun, and any modal the ASV writes as a separate word, belong to the infinitive, exactly as rule 17 keeps a subject pronoun with its verb and as the corpus does after any preposition — `לָמוּת` → *that he should die*, `מִתִּתִּי` → *that* on the preposition beside *should give* on the infinitive. The two units may interleave — *that*(`מִן`) *it*(inf.) *cannot*(`מִן`) *save*(inf.) — which rule 25 allows; do not hand the preposition the subject pronoun merely to keep its unit contiguous. Where the ASV supplies no negation at all the `מִן` keeps only the complementizer. **And the negation is the `מִן`'s only where no negative morpheme stands in the clause to carry it.** Where the privative stands on an existential `אַיִן`, that particle is what the ASV's negation word realizes: it takes that word and heads on it under rule 50, while the `מִן` keeps only the complementizer the ASV has written — `מֵאֵין עוֹבֵר` → *so that none shall pass through* gives *so that* to the `מִן` and *none* to the `אַיִן`, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does, exactly as in rules 46 and 47. What the privative governs need not be an infinitive construct: an `אַיִן` with a participle or a noun after it is read the same way. **And read that as a negative morpheme, not as the lemma `אַיִן`.** Where the privative stands instead on `בְּלִי`, `בִּלְתִּי` or another negative substantive, that morpheme is what the ASV's negation word realizes and takes it, while the `מִן` keeps only the complementizer, exactly as the `אַיִן` divides above: `מִבְּלִי יְכֹלֶת יְהוָה` → ***Because*** *Jehovah was* ***not*** *able* gives *Because* to the `מִן` and *not* to `בְּלִי`, leaving the infinitive its own *was able*. What decides it is that a morpheme carrying the negation stands in the clause, which is the condition rule 40 reads in place of a lemma and the count rule 52 runs against the morphemes that could carry a function word; do not give the `מִן` a second English word on the ground that its own lemma is the privative one. **And the complementizer the `מִן` takes need not be a result one.** Where the ASV recasts the privative clause as a causal one it writes *because* or *for* in that same slot, and that word is the preposition's on the same terms as a *that* or a *so that*. But where the ASV spends a single English word on the preposition and the negative together — `מֵאֵין` → *without* — the one-English-word condition of rule 30 is met and the two share one unit instead, headed on the negation, and that sentence governs a `מִבְּלִי` the ASV renders by one word just as it governs a `מֵאֵין`.
amendments.why: Rule 48 wrote `אַיִן` where its own justification — a present morpheme takes its English before a supplied reading, as in rules 46 and 47 — is lemma-blind, so a verse meeting `מִבְּלִי` had to reason by analogy or hand the *not* to the preposition against the rule's stated principle. DEU.9.28's `מִבְּלִי יְכֹלֶת יְהוָה` → *Because Jehovah was not able* is that case: the pass split it, giving *Because* to the `מִן` and *not* to `בְּלִי`, and cited rule 48 for a sentence that names a different particle. The amendment states the condition instead of the lemma, in the same terms rule 40 uses for its own `לְ` ("Read the condition, not the lemma"), and carries the existing fusion escape hatch across to the new case so nothing is widened past rule 30. The same verse also shows the privative taking a causal *Because* rather than the *that* or *so that* the rule listed, which the rule's wording did not admit. Amendment rather than a new rule, since the over-broad sentence is inside rule 48 and a cross-reference would leave it in place for whoever reads it first. Nothing in the corpus supplied contradicts either addition: the `מִן` table shows *without* only for `מִחוּץ`, which the fusion sentence already governs, and no unit where a negative morpheme standing beside the privative is left unrepresented.

conventions: Every *neither … nor* and bare *nor* in this chapter is divided by what stands in the line the English word opens. The opening *neither* of the twin abstinence couplets at DEU.9.9 and DEU.9.18 goes to the first clause's `לֹא` under rule 14; the closing *nor* of those verses and of DEU.9.23 goes to the waw fused with that clause's own written `לֹא` under rule 35, headed on the negative; and the two *nor*s of DEU.9.27, whose lines gap the negative, go to their waws alone. The competing division — *nor* to the waw by itself with the written second `לֹא` marked unrepresented — was considered and rejected in every case, and is named in the DEU.9.9 and DEU.9.18 unit notes.

A periphrastic `הָיָה` plus participle is divided by the English the ASV writes for each morpheme. Where it writes a compound tense, the finite verb takes the subject pronoun with the auxiliary and copula and the participle keeps only its own word: `מַמְרִים הֱיִיתֶם` → *ye have been rebellious* at DEU.9.7 and DEU.9.24. Where it collapses the periphrastic into a simple past, the finite `הָיָה` keeps the subject pronoun alone and the participle takes the whole English verb phrase: `מַקְצִפִים הֱיִיתֶם אֶת־יְהוָה` → *ye provoked Jehovah to wrath* at DEU.9.22 gives *ye* to `הָיָה` and *provoked … to wrath* to the participle, headed on *wrath* under rule 44. `הָיָה` is not marked unrepresented in the collapsed case: the pronoun realizes its own person and number under rule 17.

report: All 63 candidate groups read, plus the dump end to end for the `added` cases the lemma-keyed table is blind to. No construction is analysed two ways with nothing in the source to license the difference, so patches is empty.

The loudest rows are ASV-licensed. `לְ` before the patriarchs is aligned to *to* three times in DEU.9.5 and left unrepresented four times in DEU.9.27, because the ASV writes prepositions there (*unto thy fathers to Abraham to Isaac and to Jacob*) and a bare object here (*Remember thy servants Abraham Isaac and Jacob*); rule 40 produces both. `אֵת` is unrepresented throughout except where the English verb reaches its object through a written preposition — *of* at 9.14, *against* at 9.23 — which is rule 16's first and fourth families.

Every article resolves by counting the phrase's determiners: unrepresented wherever a demonstrative, a pronominal suffix, or a coordinated phrase's first article already holds the one written determiner (9.4, 9.5, 9.6, 9.7, 9.13, 9.19, 9.25, 9.27, 9.29), aligned wherever a *the* stands before its own word. `בַּפַּעַם הַהִוא` → *that time also* (9.19) against `בָּעֵת הַהִוא` → *at the same time* (9.20) is not two analyses of one construction: 9.20 writes both an *at* and a *the*, and 9.19 writes neither.

`מִן` + `פָּנֶה` is split wherever the ASV writes *from before* (9.4 twice, 9.5) and fused wherever it writes one word (9.19 → *of*). That is rule 30's one-rendering condition applied uniformly, not a split.

Two head choices point opposite ways and both are rule 31's subtraction test working: `מַסֵּכָה` → *a molten image* heads on *molten* (9.12), `חֵמָה` → *hot displeasure* heads on *displeasure* (9.19), because the ASV writes *displeasure* alone for that lexeme and never writes *image* alone for `מַסֵּכָה`. Do not level these to each other.

The four `added` units hold, and I audited the converse the table cannot show. *even* at 9.9 and 9.11 stands before an appositive no marker marks (9.9 writes no marker at all), which is rule 16's explicit ruling; *was written* at 9.10 is a wholly supplied lexical verb in a clause whose Hebrew has no verb morpheme; the second *it* at 9.21 answers to no object morpheme. The nearest supplied word folded in rather than marked `added` is the *say* of *hast heard say* at 9.2, and it differs on rule 20's own stated boundary — a verb morpheme is present there — with the competing reading named in its unit note.
DEU.9.28 unit 5 (`אֲשֶׁר … מִשָּׁם` → *whence*, three morphemes) is rule 22's `wherein` case verbatim and is not oversized.

BSB: no genuine error. The Td/To/R bulk disagreements are the documented convention difference. Of the two singletons, 9.19 `בַּ` is unrepresented because the ASV writes no *at* in *that time also* (contrast 9.20, where it does), and 9.26 `י` is rule 57's lexicalized suffix in `אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה` → *O Lord Jehovah*.

One amendment: rule 48 names `אַיִן` where its own reasoning means any negative morpheme, which DEU.9.28's `מִבְּלִי` → *Because … not* meets. No promotions: the periphrastic `הָיָה` division has one informative instance here, which is not a basis for a rule, so it is logged as a convention instead.
